Build a problem from a deSolve-style ODE model

Source: R/ode.R
pinn_ode.Rd

Turns an ordinary differential equation written for deSolve::ode() into a pinn_problem(). The same derivative function can be used to solve the system (a forward problem) or, with unknown and data, to estimate its parameters from observations.

Usage

pinn_ode(
  func,
  y0,
  times,
  parms = NULL,
  unknown = NULL,
  positive = TRUE,
  data = NULL,
  time = "time",
  hard_initial = TRUE
)

Arguments

func

A derivative function function(t, y, parms) in deSolve style. See Writing the model.

y0

Named numeric vector of initial states at the first time.

times

Numeric vector of times. Only its range is used for training; the full vector becomes the default grid for predict().

parms

Named numeric vector or list of known parameters.

unknown

Named numeric vector of initial guesses for parameters to estimate. These are passed to func alongside parms.

positive

Logical; see pinn_problem().

data

Optional data frame of observations with a column named as time and one column per observed state. The output of deSolve::ode() converted with as.data.frame() works directly.

time

Name of the time variable. The default, "time", matches the column name in deSolve output.

hard_initial

Logical; enforce the initial state exactly. See Initial conditions.

Value

A pinn_problem() object.

Writing the model

func has the usual deSolve signature function(t, y, parms) and returns a list whose first element holds the derivatives, in the order of y0. The recommended style works unchanged:

function(t, y, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(y, parms)), {
    dS <- -beta * S * I
    ...
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}

Indexing with y["S"], y[1] or parms["beta"] also works. Because the states are torch tensors, the body must use arithmetic and maths functions; if, ifelse, max and pmin on states do not work. Forcing functions of time can be written with tensor operations, for example torch_sin(t) or sin(t).

Initial conditions

By default the initial state is enforced exactly by writing each state as \(y(t) = y_0 + \frac{t - t_0}{t_1 - t_0} N(t)\), where \(N\) is the network. This removes one loss term and usually speeds up training. Set hard_initial = FALSE to use a soft penalty instead.

Examples

# Logistic growth dN/dt = r N (1 - N / K)
logistic <- function(t, y, parms) {
  with(as.list(c(y, parms)), list(r * N * (1 - N / K)))
}
prob <- pinn_ode(logistic, y0 = c(N = 0.1), times = seq(0, 10, by = 0.5),
                 parms = c(r = 1, K = 1))
prob
#> <pinn_problem>
#>   Domain:     time in [0, 10]
#>   Outputs:    N
#>   Parameters: r = 1, K = 1
#>   Output transform: yes
